explainBack.question: Why can a pilot tool be 'approved' by NYC Public Schools and still not be shown to help students learn or to be free of bias?
explainBack.answer: Because the approval comes from ERMA, a review that currently checks only data privacy and security. It answers the question 'does this tool protect student data?' and nothing else. NYCPS itself says it is still building the capacity to evaluate algorithmic bias, equity effects and instructional effectiveness, so those questions simply have not been tested yet — approval proves what was reviewed, not everything a parent might hope it means.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must cite the current ERMA scope (privacy and security), the admitted gap (bias, equity, instructional effectiveness still being built), and the inference that a review only answers what it tested — all present in P005 and reinforced in P008.
explainBack.assessment: Pass. The article supplies every step of this causal chain in P005 in plain language, and P008 converts it into the practical habit of asking what a tool was reviewed for.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A parent in a suburban New Jersey district (not covered by the NYC policy) receives a permission slip saying their tenth-grader's class will use a 'district-approved' AI writing tutor, with approval described as passing the state's student-data-privacy vetting.
unseenTransfer.question: Using this article's mechanism, what should the parent conclude from 'district-approved,' and what should they ask before signing?
unseenTransfer.answer: They should conclude only that the tool passed a data-privacy check — the specific question that vetting tested. It says nothing about whether the tutor's feedback is accurate, whether it treats students equitably, or whether it improves writing. Following the article's mechanism, the parent should ask three things: who will use the tool and for what (student practice, or anything touching grades or placement?), exactly what the approval review examined, and whether any evaluation of learning value or bias exists yet. The NYC policy itself doesn't apply in New Jersey, so the local district's own rules on staff decision-use also need asking.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct transfer requires the purpose-limited-evaluation model from P005, the who-uses-it-for-what question from P007, and the jurisdiction limit from P003 preventing the reader from assuming NYC rules apply elsewhere.
unseenTransfer.assessment: Pass. The article's mechanism resolves this unseen case completely and even flags the jurisdiction boundary needed to avoid over-applying the NYC rules.
